title: The probate timeline, animated
summary: A slow, honest walk through the usual phases of probate, from opening the case to closing the estate, with every state-specific window marked as varying.

layoutNotes.16:9: Full-width horizontal timeline, month markers across, icons above, captions below.
layoutNotes.9:16: Rotate the timeline to vertical: Month 0 at top, scrolling down as the narration advances. Icons to the left, captions bottom.

scenes.voiceover: Probate is the court process of settling someone's estate. Timelines vary a lot, but here is the usual path.
scenes.visual: A horizontal line draws left to right, labeled 'Month 0' to 'Month 12+'.

scenes.voiceover: First, the will, if there is one, is filed, and the court appoints a personal representative. That often takes a few weeks.
scenes.visual: Will and petition icons glide into a courthouse; a marker lands at weeks 1 to 4.

scenes.voiceover: Next, creditors and heirs are notified. There is a set window for creditor claims, often several months.
scenes.visual: Mailbox and newspaper icons; a creditor-claims bar fills across months 1 to 4.

scenes.voiceover: The representative inventories assets, may order appraisals, and pays valid debts and taxes.
scenes.visual: A checklist of house, accounts, vehicle ticks one at a time, each with a placeholder value.

scenes.voiceover: A final income tax return is needed for the person who died. Sometimes the estate itself has to file returns too.
scenes.visual: Tax form icon with a calendar page flipping.

scenes.voiceover: When the court is satisfied, assets go to the people named in the will, or to heirs under state law.
scenes.visual: Arrows fan from one estate shape to three beneficiary icons.

scenes.voiceover: Then the estate is closed. A simple one can take under a year. A contested or complex one can take much longer.
scenes.visual: A folder slides to center and a muted 'Closed' stamp lands. Two bars compare short vs. long.

scenes.voiceover: If you are handling an estate, our checklist can help. We are glad to talk when you are ready.
scenes.visual: CTA card; no urgency graphics.

title: How a revocable living trust works
summary: A diagram-first explanation of the roles in a revocable living trust, why funding matters, and what happens at incapacity and at death.

layoutNotes.16:9: One central 'Trust' container, roles around it, assets entering from the left, beneficiaries exiting right.
layoutNotes.9:16: Container top-center, assets enter from the top, beneficiaries stacked beneath it. Role labels become a vertical list.

scenes.voiceover: A living trust is like a container you create to hold your assets.
scenes.visual: A rounded box labeled 'Trust' appears beside a person icon labeled 'You'.

scenes.voiceover: You usually wear three hats: the person who creates it, the one who manages it, and, while alive, the one who benefits.
scenes.visual: Three tags animate onto the person icon: Grantor, Trustee, Beneficiary. Family icons appear as 'later beneficiaries'.

scenes.voiceover: Then you move assets into it. This step is called funding, and it is the part people forget.
scenes.visual: House, bank, and brokerage icons slide into the container; a deed paper gets a soft stamp.

scenes.voiceover: If you become unable to manage things, the successor trustee you chose steps in, without a court.
scenes.visual: The person icon dims to 40% opacity; a second person icon labeled 'Successor' slides to the container.

scenes.voiceover: When you die, the trust assets pass to your beneficiaries as you set out, often without probate.
scenes.onScreenText: At death: assets pass as written
scenes.visual: The container opens; arrows go to family icons while a courthouse icon fades.

scenes.voiceover: Retirement accounts usually stay as they are, with a beneficiary form. A trust costs more up front. And it is revocable, so you can change it.

scenes.visual: A 401(k) icon stays outside the box with a 'beneficiary form' tag; a cost tag; a slider 'revocable' toggles.

title: The Medicaid five-year look-back, explained
summary: What Medicaid's 60-month look-back is, why it exists, what counts as a transfer, and why you should talk to an elder law attorney before moving anything.

layoutNotes.16:9: Calendar left, timeline right; penalty-period bar below the timeline.
layoutNotes.9:16: Calendar top, timeline vertical in the middle, penalty bar replaced by a stacked label. Keep 120 px bottom margin.

scenes.voiceover: If you may need nursing home care, Medicaid looks back five years at your gifts.
scenes.visual: A calendar with five years highlighted in the accent color.

scenes.voiceover: Medicare doesn't pay for long-term care. Medicaid does, but only when your assets and income are low.
scenes.onScreenText: Medicare: not long-term care. Medicaid: needs-based.
scenes.visual: A bill graphic grows; a Medicare card carries a 'limited' label; Medicaid card appears with a gauge.

scenes.voiceover: If you gave away assets in that window before applying, Medicaid can set a penalty period when it won't pay.
scenes.onScreenText: Gifts in the window can mean a penalty period
scenes.visual: A gift arrow leaves a bank; a five-year window bar; then a 'penalty period' bar extends from application date.

scenes.voiceover: Gifts to family, retitling a home, even large cash transfers may count.
scenes.visual: Three icons: gift to child, house retitle, cash transfer. Each gets a small amber dot.

scenes.voiceover: There are exceptions, for example for a spouse or a disabled child. They are technical and vary by state.
scenes.visual: Spouse-and-house icon shows 'may be exempt'; disabled-child icon with a trust shape.

scenes.voiceover: Planning early gives more choices than planning in a crisis.
scenes.visual: A timeline begins earlier; branching paths widen.

title: Special needs trust: how a gift can protect benefits
summary: Why a direct inheritance can threaten SSI and Medicaid, and how a special needs trust can hold money for extras without replacing benefits.

layoutNotes.16:9: Parent + adult child left, benefits shield center, resource meter right.
layoutNotes.9:16: Meter becomes a tall vertical thermometer on the left; trust container fills the center; captions at bottom.

scenes.voiceover: If your child receives benefits like SSI or Medicaid, a direct inheritance can put those benefits at risk.
scenes.onScreenText: Inheritance can put benefits at risk
scenes.visual: Parent and adult-child icons with a shield labeled 'benefits'.

scenes.voiceover: These programs limit the money a person can hold. For SSI, that is {{words:ssiResourceLimitIndividual}} for one person. An inheritance can push someone past it.
scenes.visual: A meter fills toward a line labeled with the configured limit; an inheritance arrow overflows the line.

scenes.voiceover: A special needs trust holds the inheritance instead, and a trustee spends it on extras.
scenes.visual: A trust container receives the inheritance arrow; a trustee icon controls an outflow valve.

scenes.voiceover: Think therapies, travel, a phone, activities. It supplements benefits. It doesn't replace them.
scenes.visual: Icons appear one at a time: therapy, plane, phone, music note.

scenes.voiceover: There are different types, depending on whose money funds it. The rules differ, including what happens to leftover funds.
scenes.visual: Two labeled containers side by side; the first-party one carries a small 'payback' tag.

scenes.voiceover: Many families also write a letter of intent, describing routines, doctors, and what makes their child happy.
scenes.visual: A handwritten-style letter draws in, line by line.

scenes.voiceover: Every situation is different. Our guide can help you prepare for a conversation with an attorney.

title: Executor vs trustee vs power of attorney: who does what

scenes.voiceover: Three roles, three different jobs. People mix them up all the time.

scenes.voiceover: An executor handles your estate after you die. They file the will, pay debts, and distribute what's left.

scenes.voiceover: A trustee manages what's inside a trust, for you while you are alive, and for your beneficiaries later.

scenes.voiceover: A power of attorney lets an agent act for you while you're alive, usually for money and property. It ends at death.

scenes.voiceover: A separate health care directive names who speaks for you on medical choices.
scenes.visual: A fourth small card slides in with a heart-and-cross icon.

scenes.voiceover: Choose people who are honest and organized, and name backups. Our guide helps.

title: Funding your trust: the six assets to retitle
summary: A trust only controls what is in it. Six asset types to check: real estate, bank accounts, brokerage accounts, retirement accounts, life insurance, and personal property.

layoutNotes.16:9: Trust container center; six assets arrive from the left and right in turn with a handle label.

scenes.voiceover: You signed the trust. Great. But a trust only controls what is in it.
scenes.visual: A trust box sits mostly empty, a faint 0% fill ring around it.

scenes.voiceover: One. Your home. This usually means a new deed, recorded in the county where the property sits.
scenes.visual: House icon slides in with a deed page being stamped.

scenes.voiceover: Two. Bank accounts. Many banks retitle the account, or add a payable-on-death name, depending on the plan.

scenes.voiceover: Three. Brokerage accounts. Typically you retitle them to the trust with your broker.
scenes.visual: Chart icon slides in with a retitle arrow.

scenes.voiceover: Four. Retirement accounts. These usually stay out of the trust. You name the beneficiary on the form. Ask before changing anything, because of taxes.

scenes.visual: A retirement icon approaches the box then stops at a 'beneficiary form' gate.

scenes.voiceover: Five. Life insurance. Review who is the beneficiary, and whether the trust should be.
scenes.visual: Shield icon with a name tag.

scenes.voiceover: Six. Everything else, like furniture, jewelry, and keepsakes. A short assignment document can cover these.
scenes.visual: A small collection of icons gathers under a single document.

title: Probate vs trust: cost and time comparison

scenes.voiceover: Probate or trust? Here is a plain comparison.
scenes.visual: Two columns appear, headers only.

scenes.voiceover: Time. Probate is court-supervised, so it often takes months to over a year. A trust can usually be settled faster, since no court has to approve each step.

scenes.visual: Two bars grow, one longer than the other, with ranges shown as soft gradients, not exact numbers.

scenes.visual: Two coin stacks; the probate stack grows later, the trust stack grows earlier.

scenes.voiceover: Privacy. Probate filings are public. Trust administration usually stays private.
scenes.visual: Open vs. closed book icons.

scenes.voiceover: Effort. A trust has to be funded and kept up to date. Skip that, and some assets may still go through probate.
scenes.visual: A trust box with a dashed gap that closes when an asset is added.

scenes.voiceover: Smaller estates may not need either. Talk to us about your numbers.

title: First 30 days after a loved one dies: a calm checklist
summary: A gentle, practical checklist for the first month: what truly cannot wait, what can wait, and when to ask for help. No pressure and no sales language.

layoutNotes.16:9: Calendar strip at the bottom, current-phase card in the center, soft background.
layoutNotes.9:16: Calendar strip at the top, phase card stacked below, large captions.

scenes.voiceover: I'm sorry you're here. If someone you love has died, there's a lot to do, but not all of it today. Let's go one step at a time.
scenes.onScreenText: Take one step at a time
scenes.visual: A soft circle expands slowly; a calendar strip with 30 days appears and stays dim.

scenes.voiceover: First few days. Get several certified copies of the death certificate. The funeral home often helps order them. You'll need them for many accounts.
scenes.visual: Calendar highlights days 1 to 3; a certificate icon duplicates to a stack.

scenes.voiceover: Secure the home, pets, and mail. Let close family and key people know. Social Security is usually notified by the funeral home.
scenes.visual: House with a key; paw icon; mail slot.

scenes.voiceover: Find the documents. Look for a will, trust, insurance policies, and account lists. If you find a will, don't change or throw it away, even if it looks old.
scenes.onScreenText: Locate the will and key papers
scenes.visual: A folder opens and papers fan out, one labeled 'will'.

scenes.voiceover: Week one to two. Speak to an attorney if there's a will or trust, a house, or complicated family. Many offer a first conversation.
scenes.onScreenText: Weeks 1 to 2: talk to an attorney if needed
scenes.visual: Calendar highlights days 4 to 14; speech bubbles between two people.

scenes.voiceover: Keep paying essential bills, like mortgage or rent, utilities, and insurance, so nothing lapses. Keep a log of what you pay and why.
scenes.visual: Bill icons with check marks; a notebook log.

scenes.voiceover: Week three to four. Ask for life insurance claim forms, and check retirement accounts for named beneficiaries. Avoid moving money out of the person's accounts yet.
scenes.onScreenText: Weeks 3 to 4: claim forms and beneficiary checks
scenes.visual: Calendar highlights days 15 to 30; forms with checks.

scenes.voiceover: Don't rush big decisions. Selling the house, distributing items, or paying heirs early can create problems later.
scenes.visual: A hand-shaped pause icon over a house and gift boxes.

scenes.voiceover: Court filings, if needed, usually start within weeks to months, and deadlines vary by state. A professional can tell you which apply.
scenes.visual: Courthouse icon with a flexible-window bar labeled 'varies'.

scenes.voiceover: Look after yourself too. Ask for help. People usually want to.
scenes.visual: Two hands holding a small light.

scenes.voiceover: Our checklist keeps all of this in one place. And when you are ready, we're glad to talk.
scenes.visual: CTA card; no urgency, no phone bubble animation.

title: Estate tax thresholds explained
summary: The federal estate tax exemption for 2026, how portability works for married couples, and why some states have their own, lower thresholds. Config-driven; re-render every year.

scenes.voiceover: Only the amount above that is taxed, at rates that top out at {{pctWords:topEstateTaxRate}}.
scenes.visual: A thin slice above the line is shaded; a '40%' tag on it.

scenes.voiceover: For married couples, portability lets a surviving spouse use the unused part of the first spouse's exemption, but you generally have to file a return to elect it.

State estate/inheritance taxes and thresholds vary; do not state any in the video.

title: How a blended-family plan can protect a spouse and children
summary: Why default rules and simple 'everything to my spouse' plans can disinherit children from a prior relationship, and how trusts can balance both.

layoutNotes.16:9: Two family clusters on the left and right, a house in the center, arrows showing flow.
layoutNotes.9:16: House at center top; the two clusters stack beneath, arrows between them.

scenes.voiceover: In a blended family, the usual plan can backfire. Meet Pat, who remarried and has two kids from before.
scenes.onScreenText: Blended family: the usual plan can backfire
scenes.visual: Three circles: Pat, a new spouse, two kids from before; a house in the center.

scenes.voiceover: Pat leaves everything to the new spouse, trusting them to take care of the kids later.
scenes.visual: Arrow from Pat's estate fully into the spouse's circle.

scenes.voiceover: But once it's the spouse's, the spouse decides. A new will, a new partner, even a fair decision, and the kids may get nothing.
scenes.onScreenText: Once it's theirs, it's their choice
scenes.visual: The spouse's circle gets a new will icon with arrows pointing elsewhere; the kids dim.

scenes.voiceover: The reverse also happens. Pat leaves everything to the kids, and the spouse may lose the home.
scenes.visual: Arrows go to the kids; the spouse's house icon fades.

scenes.voiceover: A trust can split the roles. The spouse gets income, or use of the home, for life. After that, what remains goes to the children.
scenes.visual: A trust box sends a steady stream to the spouse; a valve at the end opens to the kids.

scenes.voiceover: A neutral trustee can reduce conflict. Clear writing helps too, about who pays taxes, repairs, and insurance.
scenes.visual: A balanced scale between the two clusters; a short list appears.

scenes.voiceover: Beneficiary forms, a prenup, and titling matter just as much, because they can override the plan.
scenes.onScreenText: Forms and titles can override the plan
scenes.visual: Form and deed icons float over the plan and a small arrow shows them taking priority.

scenes.voiceover: Every family is different. A short conversation can show you the options.
scenes.visual: CTA card.
